STOCKHOLM, Oct 15 : Telecom gear maker Ericsson on Thursday reported a smaller-than-expected drop in third-quarter core profit as efficiency measures helped offset higher component costs, but warned that such costs would affect margins next year.  • Operating profit before amortisation and restructuring costs was 10.1 billion crowns ($1.01 billion) against a year-earlier 15.8 billion and a mean forecast of 7.87 billion in a poll of analysts provided by Ericsson • The Swedish group said component costs rose in the quarter • "Looking ahead, the RAN (Radio Access Network) market is flat, geopolitical uncertainty remains elevated and component costs are a headwind to gross margin," new CEO Per Narvinger said in a statement

Oct 15 : Dutch digital mapping specialist TomTom NV said on Thursday it would cut 200 jobs globally as part of a reorganisation expected to generate annualised savings of about €21 million ($23.6 million). The company, which has been investing lately in its new mapping platform, TomTom Orbis, is gradually shifting its focus towards partnerships to develop new driving solutions, working with Microsoft on generative AI and with Mitsubishi Electric on automated driving, among others. "We see significant growth opportunities in automated driving and location intelligence, driven by AI," CEO Mike Schoofs said in a statement. TomTom raised its 2026 operating margin guidance to around 4 per cent from 3 per cent previously, including the impact of a €15 million restructuring charge in the fourth quarter.

BENGALURU, Oct 15 : Figma's CFO said on Thursday it was uncertain if the design software firm would return to peak gross margin levels as it ramps up AI spending, but said the investments will help draw users and better compete with sophisticated tools from labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. The company has been spending heavily on AI features, including its Figma design assistant and tools that can create prototypes and web applications using text prompts, which have helped drive a steady surge in revenue, but weighed on margins. "Are we going to get back to the low-90s gross margin percentage? I don't know. But is that the thing I would be acutely focused on? No," CFO Praveer Melwani told the Reuters Global Markets Forum on the sidelines of the company's Config user conference in Bengaluru, India. Figma's quarterly gross profit margins have shrunk to the mid-80 per cent range over the past year, down from above 90 per cent historically.

The company is betting that sacrificing margins now to boost AI adoption will help expand its user base and eventually give it room to raise prices. Figma earlier this year moved to a usage-based pricing model for AI credits on its platform. The monetization effort is expected to deliver stronger earnings in the upcoming quarters. Investors, however, have been scrutinizing finances at tech companies as they assess the returns on costly AI bets. Those concerns, coupled with worries over AI-driven disruptions, have dragged Figma's stock down about 43 per cent this year. "I would be willing to take the hit on margin the same way that we did over the last year if it means that we're able to serve a much larger total addressable market," Melwani said. "What may be good for us may not always be what an investor is looking for... We know we're going to have the ability to take price at the right point." At Config India, Figma announced expanded access to its code layers tool, new collaborative features, and partnerships with agent platforms including OpenCode, Meta Muse and India's Sarvam AI. FAST

BANGKOK, Oct 15 : Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday. Jihad Azour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told reporters the war was imposing a highly uneven economic shock to the broader region, with directly affected states under severe pressure. "The outlook depends critically on how quickly energy production and trade normalize, and on countries’ ability to preserve macroeconomic stability," Azour said at a news conference during the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. Pre-war surpluses, alternative routes, demand adjustments and substantial inventory drawdowns had helped contain the impact of the energy shock caused by the US-Israeli-led attacks on Iran and Tehran's subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

"These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments," he said. The global lender is forecasting a deep contraction of 1.3 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region after growth of 3.3 per cent in 2025, followed by a strong, but uneven rebound in 2027, when growth is expected to hit 6.6 per cent, Azour said, noting substantial differences across the region. Oil-exporting countries directly affected by the war would see a significant contraction in 2026 and a sharp rebound in growth in 2027 as energy production normalizes, but output was expected to remain below pre-war medium-term projections. The economies of oil-importing countries in the region had been resilient and were expected to remain so, he said. The Caucasus and Central Asia region had weathered the shock relatively well and inflation was expected to continue declining from elevated levels. The IMF is projecting growth to slow to 5.2 per cent in 2026 and then 5 per cent in 2027, from growth of 6.2 per cent in 2025. Azour said policymakers should prioritize price stability, focus on rebuilding fiscal buffers and expand their capacity to withstand future shocks.

Source: Reuters

FAST

TOKYO, Oct 15 : Some of Japan's largest asset managers are expected to unveil plans to buy more domestic bonds with markets focusing on whether they would step up divestments of overseas assets to bring money back home. Although a major reallocation is unexpected, consistent flows home could put a floor under the yen, analysts say, and would come at a time when shifts in Japanese demand are being closely watched because they can move foreign markets. A possible repatriation of some of the large amounts of capital deployed overseas has been under the spotlight in recent months as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government scrambled to shore up the yen, which dropped to a 40-year low in July. Japanese life insurers manage about $2.5 trillion in assets, about a quarter of which is held overseas, according to the Life Insurance Association of Japan. Several firms have lately signalled that they were eyeing domestic bonds as yields surged.

"I don't believe there is a trend toward repatriation in terms of divesting from foreign bonds to buy JGBs right now," said Keita Matsumoto, head of financial markets at SMBC Nikko Securities. "(Life insurers) are cautiously increasing their exposure to JGBs ... Their approach remains one of buying on dips as yields rise." Ministry of Finance figures show Japanese investors have made net foreign bond sales topping 5 trillion yen ($32 billion) this year, about 289 billion yen worth of which came from life insurers. In Japan, 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yields, which until little more than two years ago were capped by the central bank, have tripled to soar past 3 per cent for the first time in three decades. Domestic insurers may also step up buying 30-year JGBs as yields consolidate around 4 per cent, while increases in hedge ratios may be a precursor to selling foreign bonds, said Shoki Omori, Deutsche Bank's chief fixed-income strategist for Japan. "They will stay measured while the BOJ is still raising rates," Omori said. "Some will let hedged foreign bonds run off as they mature. What I do not expect is a broad move to sell foreign bonds and bring the money back into yen."   "Higher yields have brought the buyers back to JGBs," he added. "They have not brought the money home." 'TOO EARLY TO STEP IN' Nippon Life, Meiji Yasuda Life and Daiichi Life, which collectively manage nearly 220 trillion yen in assets, are among insurers that are expected to unveil their investment plans next week. Inflation, rising sovereign debt and growth expectations boosted by the AI boom have driven yields sharply higher across the developed world this year. In Japan, Takaichi's spending plans and tax-cut pledge have also added to market concerns. A year ago, major Japanese life insurers flagged that they expected to trim their yen-denominated bond holdings and subsequent rises in yields across the curve indicate the market has not found a bottom yet. Japanese institutions that slashed JGB holdings during the negative-interest-rate era are embarking on a gradual reappraisal of their home market, said Tetsuji Hayashi, a product specialist in Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management's investment department. "We are starting to see a shift back toward yen bonds," Hayashi said. "As interest rates rise, the 10-year JGB yield has surpassed the FX-hedged 10-year US Treasury yield." The Bank of Japan raised its key rate to a 31-year high last month and many analysts expect the central bank to raise interest rates again by the end of this year amid persistent concerns over broadening price pressures and yen weakness. Worries about supply-and-demand dynamics remain across the JGB spectrum as the BOJ reduces its bond holdings and tightens policy while the country's finances remain shaky, said an asset management official at a major life insurance company. Bond yields in Japan have risen to "fairly attractive levels," but they have yet to peak, said the official, who asked not to be identified as they were not authorised to speak to the media. "It is still too early to step in," the official said. "The Bank of Japan is not done raising rates, and fiscal concerns have not cleared up either." ($1 = 158.2900 yen)

(Additional reporting by Noriyuki Hirata. Writing by Tom Westbrook; Editing by Sumeet Chatterjee and Thomas Derpinghaus)

Source: Reuters

LONDON, Oct 15 : The Financial Stability Board (FSB), a global standard setter, has called for greater human oversight of agentic AI in final guidance for banks and other firms on managing the technology's risks.  The FSB's guidance, published Thursday, comes as regulators ramp up efforts to contain growing AI risks including the threat of AI-enabled cyber attacks, Reuters reported this week.  • In draft guidance published in June, which it "strongly encouraged" boards to refer to, the FSB warned that AI agents - which can plan and execute tasks with limited human oversight - pose distinct challenges for human oversight • Publishing its final guidance, the group said it had strengthened its recommendations on agentic AI, citing feedback on the draft, growing interest among financial institutions in adopting the technology, and the distinct risks and controls it entails

Instead, firms should recognise that "AI agents do not reason like humans and may interpret pre-defined goals in unexpected ways."

FAST

Bank of Japan board member Junko Koeda said on Thursday (Oct 15) the central bank should not become overly cautious about raising interest rates given considerable upside risks to inflation. Koeda said Japan's financial conditions remain accommodative even after the central bank's past interest rate hikes, with little sign higher borrowing costs were hurting household and business activities. Continued price increases across a wide range of consumer items suggest that underlying inflation is becoming anchored around the BOJ's 2 per cent target, she said. With wages also rising steadily, Japan appears to be making more durable progress towards sustained inflation, Koeda said. "The BOJ should adjust interest rates in a timely manner with an eye on the economic and price situation, while keeping in mind the estimated range of the neutral interest rate," she said in a speech delivered to business leaders in Kumamoto, southern Japan. The BOJ raised its key rate to a 31-year high last month, and signalled a shift toward preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its target, bolstering expectations of further policy tightening. While the BOJ may pause in October, it is likely to drop hawkish hints that would reinforce dominant market expectations of a December hike, sources have told Reuters.

Oct 15 : Oil prices fell more than 1 per cent on Thursday as investors weighed risks to supply from attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz against US efforts to cut petroleum shipping costs by easing sanctions on vessels. Brent crude futures fell $1.76, or 1.7 per cent, to $104.3 a barrel by 0625 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $1.06, or 1.1 per cent, to $94.03, reversing gains from the previous session. WTI rose to a three-week high in the prior session after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters and Tehran said it was deploying new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz and keep oil prices high. A container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank near the strait in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.

Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. With the Iran war having disrupted shipping and driven up freight costs to record highs, the Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow-fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela to help ease prices, a US official said on Wednesday. The new talks centre on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. Increased output from Russia and the Middle East has kept a lid on prices. Russia's crude oil production rose by 65,000 barrels per day in September to 8.43 million bpd but remained down 870,000 bpd year on year, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday. The IEA also said crude oil exports from Middle East Gulf producers rose by 4.4 million bpd in September to around 75 per cent of prewar levels. "While there is little concrete evidence of a near-term peace deal, oil continues to find its way to buyers through alternative routes and logistical arrangements," said Phillip Nova's head of market insights, Priyanka Sachdeva, in a client note. "These workarounds have helped prevent a more severe supply shock, although they come at a higher cost and leave global flows vulnerable to further disruption." In the US, crude oil and distillate inventories fell, while gasoline stocks rose last week, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Crude stocks fell by 11.1 million barrels in the week ended October 9, sources said. That was a much bigger draw than analysts polled by Reuters expected. "Despite the sharp inventory draw, oil prices barely reacted. The failure to rise on bullish news suggests investors are cautious about chasing prices higher at current levels," said Haitong Futures in a note on Thursday. Official numbers from the US Energy Information Administration are due at 12 p.m. EDT (1600 GMT), delayed by a day following the Columbus Day holiday on Monday.

NEW YORK/SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 14 : Anthropic told prospective investors on Wednesday that revenue in the third quarter surged 45 per cent from the prior quarter, two people who attended an investor day said, a move that could assuage market concerns about the huge costs of developing AI systems. Third-quarter revenue rose to $16.8 billion from $11.6 billion in the second quarter and $4.7 billion in the first quarter, the people said. Anthropic told the group the company was profitable on an adjusted basis in the third quarter, they added.  The meeting in San Francisco was meant to familiarize prospective Anthropic investors with the company before its highly anticipated IPO. The IPO is expected to precede a public listing by rival OpenAI, making Anthropic an early test of investor appetite for loss-making AI developers investing heavily to pursue massive scale. Its public-market debut is likely to be pushed until after the November US midterm elections, Reuters has reported.

Attendees at Wednesday's event met with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and came away optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability, a few of them told Reuters as they left its headquarters in the evening.  Amodei reiterated the company’s focus on AI safety but avoided mentioning threats of human extinction, one person in the group said. In its prospectus seen by Reuters last month, Anthropic warned that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."  On Wednesday, however, Anthropic executives talked about how the company was using its AI to help its own business including designing a custom chip. The company handed out hats to the attendees, some of which read "thinking." Anthropic could see its annual revenue run rate reach $110 billion by the end of the year, according to estimates from analysts who met with company executives earlier this week. Anthropic did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. Scrutiny of AI companies' finances has intensified as they pour money into chips, data centers and computing power needed to develop and operate increasingly powerful models. Targeting a valuation of over $2 trillion, Anthropic is seeking to convince investors that its breakneck revenue growth can eventually outrun the enormous costs of building and running AI systems. Last year, Anthropic's revenue increased twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion, even as the company lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis, excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising, Reuters reported exclusively last month.  The company has committed at least $518 billion over a decade for cloud services, computing and infrastructure. Founded by former OpenAI executives, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models. Its expansion has been underpinned by Alphabet's Google and Amazon, which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors. Anthropic has also sought to distinguish itself through its focus on AI safety, warning of the dangers posed by increasingly capable systems even as it competes in the race to develop and commercialize more powerful models. Its research has found that its own AI agents have engaged in troubling behavior in test environments, including leaking sensitive information and sabotaging code, though the company has said it has not seen evidence of such misalignment in real-world deployments. The Financial Times first reported the third-quarter revenue figure on Wednesday.

Oct 14 : A group of 40 state attorneys general on Wednesday urged a US bankruptcy judge in Delaware to protect young users of Character.AI and keep their data safe during the AI companion company's bankruptcy. Character.AI filed for bankruptcy late on Monday and is seeking to use its Chapter 11 case to resolve the states' investigations and lawsuits, license its technology to Disney for $20 million, and seek a buyer willing to take on its chatbot business.  Abigail Ryan, an attorney for the states, told US Bankruptcy Judge Brendan Shannon in Wilmington that the states are negotiating a settlement with Character.AI over allegations that its chatbots impersonated licensed medical professionals and exposed children to sexualized and abusive interactions. Even so, Ryan said, the states want to make sure that any buyer of Character.AI's assets will protect users' chat histories and improve safety features.

"We're willing to work with the buyers to find safeguards, but we don't want to see what has transpired in the past start over with a new purchaser," Ryan said at the company's first hearing in US bankruptcy court. "This company has collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder," New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, said in a Wednesday statement issued just before the court hearing.   NO OFFER YET Character.AI's attorney, Erin Fay, said she heard those concerns "loud and clear," but said that no buyer has yet made an offer for the company's user data or its operating chatbot business. The company's platform allows users to interact with and create generative AI characters customized by user prompts and often modeled on fictional characters, celebrities, and historical figures. Its active users spend an average of two hours a day talking to the chatbots. Beyond the states' claims, Character.AI has been sued by families who allege that its chatbots gave harmful advice, contributed to the suicides of two children, and exposed children to sexualized and bullying interactions. Character.AI has reached preliminary settlements with five of those families. The company also faces investigations by the US government and by authorities in the UK, Italy, Russia and Australia. Disney has agreed to pay $20 million to license the company's technology and intellectual property, as well as hiring most of Character.AI's staff, but is not interested in the type of data that the state AGs are worried about, Fay said. Disney's asset purchase must be approved by the bankruptcy court, and it is subject to higher offers. Fay described a grim mood within the company in recent months, saying that employees "were very excited about the product and the user base" but had "lost faith in the company's trajectory." The company attributed its bankruptcy to legal expenses and the high price for computing power and AI talent, saying it was losing between $8 million and $9 million a month before filing for Chapter 11 protection.  Character.AI's management became concerned about its ability to survive employee attrition by late summer. In September, Disney stepped in to hire most of the company's employees and allow them to work on keeping Character.AI afloat during a bankruptcy sale process and technology transition, according to court filings.

Oct 14 : A US biotech company says it is making progress toward its goal of resurrecting the dodo, the famous flightless bird with a large hooked beak, and returning it to its native Indian Ocean island of Mauritius, where humans drove it to extinction in the 17th century. Dallas-based Colossal Biosciences said on Wednesday it has used a newly developed AI platform to identify genetic changes that may be responsible for the dodo's distinctive craniofacial traits as its scientists pursue gene-editing targets to bring back this lost species. Colossal is planning to perform gene-editing to bring dodo traits into the cells of its closest living relative, the Nicobar pigeon. Native to some Southeast Asian islands, the Nicobar pigeon is known for its shimmering green and copper feathers and, unlike the dodo, can fly. The company said it is in the final stages of its analysis of the dodo genome, now filled to 95 per cent. It also said it has made an advance that should shorten the time needed to test whether a genetic edit produces the desired trait. The company did not announce a timeframe for hatching a dodo.

Colossal says it is dedicated to "de-extinction" — resurrecting vanished species. Last year, it said it had genetically engineered the dire wolf by editing the genes of the gray wolf, the extinct Ice Age predator's closest living relative, to add dire wolf traits. Besides the dodo and dire wolf, Colossal has four other species on its de-extinction list: the woolly mammoth; the thylacine, also called the Tasmanian tiger; the bluebuck antelope; and the moa, a large flightless bird. "The dodo is the world's best-known symbol of extinction caused by people. It disappeared within decades of humans arriving on Mauritius, largely because of the introduction of invasive species like rats and other animals they brought. Bringing it back shows extinction doesn't have to be permanent," Ben Lamm, Colossal's CEO and co-founder, told Reuters. "The big hurdles ahead are proving which genetic changes really matter, making many of those edits in a bird and passing them to the next generation, and preparing a safe home for dodos on Mauritius," Lamm said. The dodo was a ground-nesting bird about 3 feet (1 metre) tall and weighing up to about 50 pounds (23 kg). Having never encountered humans, dodos exhibited no fear of the people who reached Mauritius in the 16th century. Pressured by invasive species and human hunting, the last living dodo was seen in 1662. It has remained alive in popular culture including in Lewis Carroll's book "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland." GENOMORPH PLATFORM Ancient DNA is always broken into small pieces, so no ancient genome is perfectly complete, including that of the dodo. The new AI platform Colossal built is called GenoMorph. "The challenge was scientists only have one complete dodo genome, making it difficult to distinguish the genetic differences that made the dodo unique from ordinary genetic variation. GenoMorph effectively acts as a 'treasure map' for the dodo genome, narrowing hundreds of thousands of possible genetic changes into the targets most likely to explain its iconic beak and facial structure," Lamm said. Beth Shapiro, Colossal's chief science officer, said GenoMorph finds likely gene-editing targets for species with very little surviving DNA. Normally scientists compare many genomes from one species to find the genes behind a trait, but this is not possible with the dodo, Shapiro said. "So instead, GenoMorph studies how skulls and beaks develop across more than 70 living bird species and learns which genetic switches control their shape. It gave us a shortlist of about 2,300 candidates linked to beak size and shape. These targets are now being validated in the lab," Shapiro said. Colossal said it has expanded its colony of Nicobar pigeons in Texas to 36 birds following successful breeding among established pairs. It said this should help in studying Nicobar pigeon development, reproduction and genetics. Lamm said the company is working with Mauritian scientists, conservation groups and the Mauritius government on what bringing the dodo back to its native land might look like. "Getting Mauritius ready for dodos also means removing invasive predators and restoring habitat, which helps the native species living there now," Lamm said. "No release sites will be chosen until the ecological work and community consultation are finalized, but it is Colossal's goal to put our dodos back into their natural habitats in Mauritius."

Source: Reuters
